content: A spasm is defined as a sudden, involuntary contraction of a muscle, a group of muscles, a hollow organ, or an orifice. This contraction may sometimes be accompanied by a sudden burst of pain. However, in most cases, it is harmless and resolves on its own within a few minutes. Spasmodic muscle contractions can also occur as a result of various medical conditions, including dystonias, which are disorders characterized by involuntary muscle contractions. Beyond its physiological definition, the term spasm can also refer to a sudden and temporary surge of energy, activity, or emotion. In certain cases, spasms can affect hollow organs, such as the bile duct. A common feature of colic, which involves spasms in such organs, is the sensation of needing to move around to alleviate discomfort. Severe colic-related pain may lead to nausea or vomiting. When spasms occur in a series or become persistent, the condition is referred to as spasmism. In extreme cases, spasms can cause muscular contractions that are more forceful than what the individual could normally produce. Such intense contractions may result in torn tendons or ligaments. Some experts suggest that hysterical strength, a phenomenon where individuals exhibit extraordinary physical strength in extreme situations, may be a type of spasm triggered by the brain under conditions of intense stress or danger.
